This page demonstrates the estimators that `py-qte` offers for distributional
difference-in-differences. The available estimators are

1. Changes-in-changes ([Athey & Imbens 2006](#ref-ai-2006)),
2. Quantile difference-in-differences ([Athey & Imbens 2006](#ref-ai-2006), Section 3.3),
3. Mean difference-in-differences, and
4. Distributional difference-in-differences ([Callaway, Li & Oka 2018](#ref-clo-2018)).

All four follow the approach of [Callaway & Sant'Anna 2021](#ref-cs-2021) in that they allow an
arbitrary number of groups and time periods, but the actual effects are estimated per treated
group-time cell relative to a single comparison (_pre-treatment_) period and a single control group.
The estimators offer various ways to determine the comparison group and period. As in
[Callaway & Sant'Anna 2021](#ref-cs-2021), aggregation procedures are offered which give treatment
effects at higher levels than the individual group-time cells of the treated. The available
aggregations are described [here](aggregation.qmd).

The object of interest in what follows is the _entire_ distribution of $Y^{d=0}(d=1,t=T)$, i.e. the
potential outcome under no treatment (as indicated by the superscript $d=0$) for a group that was in
fact treated, i.e. $d=1$, at period $T$.

The available estimators differ in under what assumptions this counterfactual distribution is
derived from observables. The following sections give a brief description of each estimator and the
underlying identification assumptions, together with showing how the corresponding estimation can be
performed with the `py-qte` package and how to present the results.

{{< include _setup-did.qmd >}}

@lst-config displays what quantiles are computed throughout and the configuration of the boostrap.

```{python}
#| label: lst-config
from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig

QS = [0.25, 0.50, 0.75]
BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=50, seed=42, n_workers=4)
```

## The Data

The demonstration data are county-level teen employment in the United States from 2003 to 2007,
together with whether a county's minimum wage was raised above the federal minimum. The dataset
contains three treatment groups identified by the year in which the respective county was initially
treated (2004, 2006, 2007). There is also a group of counties that was never treated. The panel is
balanced: 500 counties observed in each of the five years.

The outcome of interest is `lemp`, the natural logarithm of the number of employed teenagers in the
county. Because it is a count and not a rate, its level also reflects how large a county is, and
differences in county size across the treatment groups are visible in the averages below.

```{python}
#| label: lst-did-data
from qte.datasets import load_mpdta

GROUP_LABEL = (
    pl.col("group")
    .replace(float("inf"), None)
    .cast(pl.Int64)
    .cast(pl.String)
    .fill_null("never treated")
    .alias("Group")
)

# `first.treat` is 0 for counties that never raised their minimum wage; the estimators expect
# +inf for never-treated units, which is what the default of `TrtGroupConfig` assumes.
panel = load_mpdta().with_columns(pl.col("first.treat").replace(0, float("inf")).alias("group"))
print(f"{panel.height:,} county-year observations for {panel['countyreal'].n_unique()} counties")
print(f"years: {panel['year'].unique().sort().to_list()}")
```

@tbl-did-means reports the average log teen employment by treatment group and year. We see that
there are large differences in the outcome variable even under no treatment. This suggests that a
simple comparison between the treated group and a control group will not successfully identify
treatment effects on the treated group. The distributional difference-in-differences estimators can
address some of the potential confounding.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-did-means
#| echo: false
from great_tables import GT, loc, style

means = (
    panel.pivot(on="year", index="group", values="lemp", aggregate_function="mean")
    .sort("group")
    .with_columns(GROUP_LABEL)
)
means = means.select("Group", *[c for c in means.columns if c not in ("group", "Group")])
years = [c for c in means.columns if c != "Group"]

# A cell is treated once the group has been treated by that year. The never-treated counties are
# never treated, and the years before a group's first treated year are not yet treated.
means_table = (
    GT(means)
    .tab_header(title="Average log teen employment by treatment group and year")
    # Row striping would add a third background colour on top of the two below.
    .opt_row_striping(row_striping=False)
    .tab_footnote(
        footnote="Group is the first year in which the county's minimum wage exceeded the federal "
        "minimum.",
        locations=loc.column_labels(columns="Group"),
    )
    # Keep the table (and with it the footnote block) flush with the left margin of the text.
    .tab_options(table_margin_left="0px", table_margin_right="auto")
)
for row in means.iter_rows(named=True):
    treated_from = None if row["Group"] == "never treated" else int(row["Group"])
    for year in years:
        treated = treated_from is not None and int(year) >= treated_from
        means_table = means_table.tab_style(
            style=style.fill(color="#fde68a" if treated else "#e5e7eb"),
            locations=loc.body(columns=year, rows=pl.col("Group") == row["Group"]),
        )

means_table.tab_source_note(
    "Yellow cells are years in which the group is treated; grey cells are not treated, which "
    "includes the years before a group is treated and the never-treated counties throughout."
).fmt_number(years, decimals=3)
```

## Changes-in-Changes

The Changes-in-Changes (CIC) model was developed by [Athey & Imbens 2006](#ref-ai-2006). The crucial
assumptions are that the outcomes under no treatment — if the causal target of interest is an effect
on the treated — are determined by a “production function”, $Y^{d=0}=h(U,t)$, that depends on time,
$t$, and on a _single_ unobserved index of individual-level characteristics, $U$.

The production function is assumed to be monotone in that index, and it is indexed by neither group
membership nor the individual observation $i$. The distribution of $U$ is unrestricted across groups
but, within a group, does not change over time. It is further assumed that the latent
characteristics satisfy a common support assumption across groups.

So this model, intuitively, assumes that _in the absence of the treatment_ two individuals from
different groups _with the same latent characteristic_ $U=u$ display the exact same evolution of
outcomes. This, together with the assumption of common support, suggests that one can indeed
identify the counterfactual distribution of the outcomes of the treated under no treatment in the
post-treatment period.

Formally, under the assumptions of the CIC model this counterfactual distribution is generated by
the following transformation, applied to the outcomes of the treated in the pre-treatment period.

$$
k_{CIC}(y) = F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=1)}\!\left(F_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=0)}(y)\right).
$$

@lst-cic shows how to use this estimator in `py-qte`.

```{python}
#| label: lst-cic
from qte.distributional_did import estimate_changes_in_changes_effects

with timer("changes-in-changes"):
    cic = estimate_changes_in_changes_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

@tbl-cic and @fig-cic show the results in tabular and graphical form.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cic
cic.overall.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-cic
#| fig-cap: "Changes-in-Changes: quantile treatment effects on the overall aggregation."
show_chart(cic.overall.plot())
```

## Quantile Difference-in-Differences

The Quantile Difference-in-Differences (QDID) model is motivated by the idea that the observed
evolution of a quantile $q$ of the (marginal) distribution of outcomes that the untreated
experienced from the pre- to the post-treatment period can act as a stand-in for the counterfactual
evolution of the same quantile that the outcome distribution of the treated would have experienced
had they not been treated.

$$
F^{-1}_{Y^{d=0}(d=1,t=1)}(q) =
F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=1,t=0)}(q) +
\left[F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=1)}(q) - F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=0)}(q)\right]
$$

The QDID model is formalized — that is, connected to a set of assumptions on primitives — in
[Athey & Imbens 2006](#ref-ai-2006), Section 3.3. They assume that
$Y^{d=0} = \tilde{h}(U,G,T) = \tilde{h}_G(U,G) + \tilde{h}_T(U,T)$, which is strictly increasing in
$U$, and that $U$ is independent of both $G$ and $T$. This model generates differences in the
distribution of $Y^{d=0}$ both across groups and across time. Intuitively, at a fixed $U$ the change
in untreated potential outcomes is identical across the two groups, which is what identifies the
counterfactual distribution in an essentially analogous way to the standard
difference-in-differences model (at a fixed $u$ the counterfactual post-treatment period outcome of
the treatment is exactly equal to the pre-treatment period outcome plus the observed change in the
outcome derived from the untreated).

Applied to each treated pre-treatment outcome rather than to one quantile at a time, the identity
above gives the following transformation:

$$
k_{QDID}(y) = y + \left[F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=1)}(q) - F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=0)}(q)\right],
\qquad q = F_{Y^{obs}(d=1,t=0)}(y).
$$

@lst-qdid shows how to use this estimator in `py-qte`.

```{python}
#| label: lst-qdid
from qte.distributional_did import estimate_quantile_did_effects

with timer("quantile difference-in-differences"):
    qdid = estimate_quantile_did_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

@tbl-qdid and @fig-qdid show the results in tabular and graphical form.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-qdid
qdid.overall.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-qdid
#| fig-cap: "Quantile Difference-in-Differences: quantile treatment effects on the overall aggregation."
show_chart(qdid.overall.plot())
```

## Mean Difference-in-Differences

Mean Difference-in-Differences (MDID) shifts the treated group's whole pre-treatment distribution by
the change in the comparison group's mean:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{Y(0)\mid D=1}(y) &= F_{Y,\text{pre}\mid D=1}(y - \Delta), \\[2pt]
\Delta &= E[Y_{\text{post}} \mid D=0] - E[Y_{\text{pre}} \mid D=0].
\end{aligned}
$$

This is stronger than the usual difference-in-differences assumption, which only requires the means
to move in parallel: here every quantile of the counterfactual distribution is the corresponding
pre-treatment quantile shifted by the same constant,
$F^{-1}_{Y^{d=0}(d=1,t=1)}(q) = F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=1,t=0)}(q) + \Delta$. In the notation of
[Athey & Imbens 2006](#ref-ai-2006) this is the transformation
$k_{DID}(y) = y + E[Y_{01}] - E[Y_{00}]$.

Relative to the QDID model, the change is not allowed to vary with $u$: in the QDID model above the
time effect can differ across quantiles, whereas here it is a single number. The quantile effects
this model reports are consequently not evidence about how effects vary across the distribution —
they are the treated group's own distributional change net of a constant, and only the average
effect rests on the identifying assumption.

@lst-mdid shows how to use this estimator in `py-qte`.

```{python}
#| label: lst-mdid
from qte.distributional_did import estimate_mean_did_effects

with timer("mean difference-in-differences"):
    mdid = estimate_mean_did_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

@tbl-mdid and @fig-mdid show the results in tabular and graphical form.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-mdid
mdid.overall.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-mdid
#| fig-cap: "Mean Difference-in-Differences: quantile treatment effects on the overall aggregation."
show_chart(mdid.overall.plot())
```

## Distributional Difference-in-Differences

The Distributional Difference-in-Differences (DDiD) model of
[Callaway, Li & Oka 2018](#ref-clo-2018) assumes that the _change in untreated potential outcomes_
has the same distribution in both groups. This, however, is not enough to identify
$F_{Y^{d=0}(d=1,t=1)}$. Intuitively, for a given pre-treatment period distribution of outcomes for
the treated, $F_{Y^{d=0}(d=1,t=0)}$, a restriction on the distribution of changes can generate many
distributions of the outcome levels of the treated group in the post-treatment period. This issue
can be remedied by imposing that the pre-treatment period levels and the changes from the pre- to
the post-treatment period move in a similar way together in the treated and in the untreated group.
Technically, it is required that the associated copula be the same in both groups.

The counterfactual distribution of interest is then given by:

$$
F_{Y(0)\mid D=1}(y) =
\Pr\left\{\Delta Y_{j} + F^{-1}_{Y_{10}}\!\left(F_{Y_{00}}(Y_{j})\right) \le y \;\middle|\; D = 0\right\},
$$

where $\Delta Y_j$ is comparison unit $j$'s own change and $Y_j$ its pre-treatment outcome.

@lst-ddid shows how to use this estimator in `py-qte`.

```{python}
#| label: lst-ddid
from qte.distributional_did import estimate_distributional_did_effects

with timer("distributional difference-in-differences"):
    ddid = estimate_distributional_did_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )
```

@tbl-ddid and @fig-ddid show the results in tabular and graphical form.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ddid
ddid.overall.tabulate(quantiles=QS)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-ddid
#| fig-cap: "Distributional Difference-in-Differences: quantile treatment effects on the overall aggregation."
show_chart(ddid.overall.plot())
```

## Summary

Finally, @tbl-did-all compares the four estimators.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-did-all
#| echo: false
estimates = {
    "Changes-in-changes": cic,
    "Quantile DiD": qdid,
    "Mean DiD": mdid,
    "Distributional DiD": ddid,
}
comparison = pl.DataFrame({"Quantile": QS})
for name, result in estimates.items():
    comparison = comparison.with_columns(
        pl.Series(name, result.overall.qtt.sort("q")["effect"].to_list())
    )
(
    GT(comparison)
    .tab_header(title="Quantile treatment effects, overall aggregation, all four estimators")
    .fmt_number([c for c in comparison.columns if c != "Quantile"], decimals=3)
)
```
